title: Peopleware
author: Tom DeMarco and Timothy Lister
theme: Most project failures are caused by how people are managed and treated, not by technology, so managers should focus on the human side of work.
summary: Tom DeMarco and Timothy Lister spent years studying software projects, and they reached a conclusion that surprised many managers. When projects fail, the cause is rarely a technical problem. It is usually a people problem: poor working conditions, careless management or teams that never come together. Peopleware argues that managers should spend far less effort on methods and tools and far more on the human beings who do the work.

The authors first attack the factory mindset that treats knowledge workers as interchangeable parts. Pushing people with pressure and overtime may look productive, but it tends to lower quality, and the lost time is quietly taken back later. People also care deeply about doing work they can be proud of, so forcing them to cut quality damages morale and commitment.

A large part of the book is about the workplace itself. Creative work depends on long stretches of deep concentration, a state that takes time to enter and is destroyed by a single interruption. Noisy open offices, constant phone calls and cramped desks keep people from ever reaching it. The authors' own coding experiments found that the best performers tended to work in quieter, more private spaces, suggesting that environment matters as much as raw talent.
The book then turns to people. Hiring well, keeping good staff and lowering turnover save far more than they cost, because each departure takes away knowledge and momentum that are slow to rebuild.

Finally, the authors examine teams. A jelled team, whose members trust one another and share a goal, produces far more than the sum of its individuals. Such teams cannot be ordered into existence, but managers can easily kill them through bureaucracy, splitting people across projects, defensive control and artificial deadlines. The manager's real job is to create conditions in which good teams can grow, and then to protect them.
takeaway: Protect people's concentration, respect their pride in quality and remove whatever stops teams from jelling.

questions.q: What is the central claim of Peopleware about why projects fail?
options: Most failures come from weak technology choices
Most failures are sociological, rooted in how people are managed
Most failures come from lack of funding
Most failures are caused by customers changing their minds
questions.why: The authors argue the major problems of project work are human and organisational rather than technical.

questions.q: Which managerial mindset do the authors criticise most strongly?
options: Treating knowledge workers as interchangeable factory parts
Giving teams too much autonomy
Investing too heavily in training
Allowing staff to work from quiet rooms
questions.why: They reject the production-line view in which people can be swapped and driven like machines.

questions.q: According to the book, what usually happens after sustained overtime?
options: Output rises permanently
Turnover falls sharply
Quality improves because people focus harder
Lost time is recovered later through reduced effort, and quality suffers
questions.why: The authors note that extra hours tend to be balanced by later slack, while errors and burnout increase.

questions.q: Why do the authors object to pressuring people to lower quality?
options: It always breaks the law
Customers never notice the difference
People's self-esteem is tied to quality work, so it harms morale
It makes estimating harder
questions.why: Workers take pride in quality, and forcing them to cut corners erodes their commitment.

questions.q: What mental state do the authors say creative work depends on?
options: Constant multitasking
Long periods of deep, uninterrupted concentration
Frequent short meetings
Competition between colleagues
questions.why: Knowledge work needs immersion that takes time to reach and is broken by interruptions.

questions.q: What did the authors' coding experiments suggest about top performers?
options: They were mostly the most experienced staff
They earned the highest salaries
They used the newest programming languages
They tended to work in quieter, more private environments
questions.why: The results linked better performance with workspaces that offered quiet and freedom from interruption.

questions.q: Why do the authors see staff turnover as so costly?
options: Each departure removes knowledge and momentum that take long to rebuild
Recruitment adverts are expensive
Leaving staff always join competitors
It increases office rent
questions.why: Replacing people means lost expertise and a long ramp-up period for newcomers.

questions.q: What is a 'jelled' team in the book's sense?
options: A team formed by a reorganisation memo
A team with the largest budget
A group whose members trust one another and share a goal, producing more than the sum of its parts
A team that works only on maintenance
questions.why: Jelled teams have strong cohesion and shared purpose, which multiplies their output.

questions.q: Which of these is described as damaging to team formation?
options: Giving teams a clear shared goal
Splitting people's time across many projects
Letting a team stay together after success
Trusting team members to manage their own work
questions.why: Fragmenting people across projects is one of the practices the authors say prevents teams from jelling.

questions.q: According to Peopleware, what is a manager's real job regarding teams?
options: To order teams to jell by a deadline
To monitor every task closely
To create the conditions in which teams can grow and then protect them
To rotate members frequently to keep things fresh
questions.why: Teams cannot be commanded into existence; managers can only nurture good conditions and remove obstacles.
